analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal-state program making community college tuition-free and cutting costs at minority-serving colleges.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 2019 with 5 cosponsors and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended in January 2021 without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have paid 75% of the cost of waiving resident tuition and fees at community colleges, with states and tribes paying the rest, so students attending at least half-time would pay nothing for tuition. It also created grants for historically black colleges, tribal colleges, and other minority-serving institutions to waive or sharply cut tuition for low-income students, and required states to make community college credits fully transferable to public four-year universities. It authorized funding rising from about $1.6 billion in 2020 to roughly $18 billion per year by 2029.
analysis.who_benefits: Students attending community college at least half-time, including those who would qualify for in-state tuition but for their immigration status, would pay $0 in tuition and fees for up to three years of benefits. Low-income students at historically black, tribal, and minority-serving four-year institutions would get tuition waived or significantly reduced for their first 60 credits. Community colleges and those institutions would receive a major new funding stream, and states would be pushed to strengthen transfer pathways so two-year credits count fully toward a bachelor's degree.

how_it_helps.text: Community college students would pay $0 in resident tuition and fees, with the federal government covering at least 75% of the average cost and states or tribes the remainder; tribes where most students are low-income would get at least 95% federal coverage.

Low-income students at historically black, tribal, and minority-serving four-year colleges would have tuition and fees waived or significantly reduced for up to 60 credits, with grants capped at the national average public four-year tuition.

States would have to create common, fully transferable general-education cores so an associate degree counts as the first two years of a related bachelor's program at any public university in the state.

Participating colleges would have to adopt supports like childcare, transportation, food assistance, mentoring, and advising, and states would need to keep funding public higher education at or above prior three-year averages.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through appropriations rising from $1.6 billion in fiscal 2020 to about $16.3 billion a year for community colleges plus up to roughly $1.6 billion a year for minority-serving institutions. Participating states and tribes would pay the remaining 25% of community college tuition costs and would have to maintain their existing per-student funding for public higher education as a condition of the grant.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates money directly, reaching roughly $18 billion per year by 2029, a large new standing federal commitment to higher education.
Students would still need to cover living costs; the bill only waives tuition and fees, and it explicitly bars using other financial aid for those waived charges.

Eligibility lasts only three calendar years after benefits begin, and requires at least half-time enrollment and satisfactory academic progress, so part-time strivers and slow finishers lose the benefit.

Some aid would go to students who would have attended anyway, and states must commit their own 25% share, which wealthier students in participating states would effectively benefit from alongside low-income ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and targeted: free community college tuition and reduced tuition at institutions serving mostly low-income students, paired with requirements that states fix broken credit transfer. The costs are real but conventional — a growing federal appropriation and a state match — and the design limits the open-ended risk with a three-year student cap, per-student rebate ceilings, and a maintenance-of-effort requirement. An honest critic would note the price grows steeply after the first two years and that waiving tuition helps middle-income students too, not just those who need it most.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again, dying in committee when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Levin introduced the bill on August 27, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day.
Five Democratic members cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
No further action was taken after the referral, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, federal taxpayers and states avoided a new multi-billion-dollar-per-year higher education commitment, and for-profit colleges avoided competing against a free public alternative. Students who would have qualified for the tuition waiver got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Andy Levin
for.role: Sponsor, House Education and Labor Committee member

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee chair
against.role: Committee chair with sole power to schedule a markup
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee vote or markup after it was referred; the bill saw no action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the chamber's actual split is unknown; all 6 initial sponsors and all 5 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: The bill routes a new federal tuition subsidy through community colleges, making them the permanent channel for free-tuition funding while imposing completion and reporting requirements on them. Students and the colleges would gain together.

industries.industry: Historically black, tribal, and minority-serving four-year colleges
industries.note: They would receive per-student grants to waive or cut tuition for low-income students, with caps tied to national average public tuition and restrictions on raising prices. Their gain is the students' gain.

A free public two-year option would draw students away from for-profit schools, which charge far higher tuition funded largely by federal aid. The industry's interest in keeping that tuition-paying enrollment runs against students' interest in a free alternative.
